title: Caribbean Stud Poker in Canada: Odds and Strategy
excerpt: Caribbean Stud looks like poker but plays like a table game. Here is the correct raise-fold strategy, the real house edge, and why the jackpot side bet costs you.
author: Jane Williams
bodyHtml:
Caribbean Stud Poker sits in an odd corner of the Canadian online casino lobby. It carries the word poker, so players expect bluffing and reads. In truth it is a five-card table game against a fixed dealer rule set, closer to blackjack in structure than to anything you would find in a poker room. There is no bluffing, no opponent psychology and no way to fold your way to profit — but there is a correct strategy, and playing it properly cuts the house edge roughly in half compared to instinct.

This guide covers how the game runs, what the numbers actually are, and the handful of decisions that separate a well-played session from an expensive one.

How a hand plays out

You place an ante. You and the dealer each receive five cards; all of yours are face up, and exactly one of the dealer's is exposed. You then make a single decision: fold and forfeit the ante, or raise by placing an additional bet of exactly twice the ante.

If you raise, the dealer reveals. Everything hinges on whether the dealer qualifies, which requires a hand of ace-king or better:

  • Dealer does not qualify: your ante pays even money and your raise pushes — returned to you without profit. This is the rule that shapes the whole game.
  • Dealer qualifies and you win: the ante pays even money and the raise pays according to a pay table based on your hand's rank.
  • Dealer qualifies and beats you: you lose both bets.
  • Tie: both bets push.

The dealer qualifies roughly 56% of the time. That means on nearly half of the hands you raise, your two-thirds-larger raise bet earns nothing at all. Understanding that asymmetry is the key to understanding why the game is priced the way it is.

The raise pay table

When the dealer qualifies and you win, the raise pays on a scale: 1 to 1 for a pair or less, 2 to 1 for two pair, 3 to 1 for three of a kind, 4 to 1 for a straight, 5 to 1 for a flush, 7 to 1 for a full house, 20 to 1 for four of a kind, 50 to 1 for a straight flush and 100 to 1 for a royal flush. Some operators cap the total payout per hand — worth checking in the game rules before you sit down, because a cap quietly removes value from the top of the table.

The house edge, honestly stated

Played with correct strategy, Caribbean Stud carries a house edge of roughly 5.2% of the ante. That number looks alarming next to blackjack, and it should be read carefully.

Because you frequently have three units in play (ante plus a double-size raise) rather than one, the edge measured against total money wagered is closer to 2.6%. That is the figure to compare against other table games — and by that measure Caribbean Stud is mid-pack: worse than well-played online blackjack, worse than the good bets in baccarat, better than most slot machines and dramatically better than keno.

The practical consequence is bankroll swing. A game that routinely puts three units at risk per hand burns through a balance faster than the edge alone suggests. Size your ante with that in mind, not the way you would size a blackjack bet.

Correct strategy: what to raise and what to fold

The full mathematically optimal strategy for Caribbean Stud is genuinely complicated, involving comparisons between your unmatched cards and the dealer's upcard. Fortunately, a simplified version captures almost all of its value and loses only a fraction of a percent in expectation.

The simple rule

  • Always raise with a pair or better. No exceptions, no matter what the dealer shows.
  • Always fold with less than ace-king. If your hand cannot beat the dealer's minimum qualifying hand, raising is throwing two extra units at a losing position.
  • With exactly ace-king high, raise if the dealer's upcard matches one of your other three cards, or if the dealer's upcard is lower than your fourth-highest card, or if the dealer shows an ace or a king and you hold a queen or a jack.

Everything else follows from that. Roughly half of all hands are folds, which surprises new players who feel they should be in the action. Folding correctly is the strategy.

The two errors that cost the most

The first is raising on junk because the ante feels wasted. It is not wasted — surrendering one unit is cheaper than risking three on a hand that cannot qualify. The second is folding a small pair against a scary dealer upcard. A pair beats a non-qualifying dealer and beats ace-king, which together cover most of the outcomes. Raise it every time.

The progressive jackpot side bet

Almost every online version offers a small side wager, typically one or five dollars, paying on your own five cards regardless of the dealer's hand — a fixed scale for flushes and full houses, a percentage of a progressive pool for a straight flush, and the full pool for a royal.

The honest assessment: this bet usually carries a house edge in the range of 20% to 30% and sometimes higher, depending on the current jackpot size. It is far and away the worst-value wager on the table. There is a theoretical point at which a large enough progressive pool tips the side bet to positive expectation, but the pools rarely reach it and the variance is brutal even when they do. Treat it as an entertainment expense and nothing else, in the same way you would a long-odds side wager anywhere else on the casino floor.

Where Canadians can play it

Caribbean Stud is a staple of the poker-derivative section at most Canadian-facing online casinos, both in RNG form and, increasingly, as a live dealer table. The live version plays slower, which is a mild advantage: fewer hands per hour means less exposure to the edge, even though the per-hand maths is identical.

Rules do vary between software providers, so read the pay table before you play. A version paying 6 to 1 rather than 7 to 1 on a full house is meaningfully worse, and payout caps matter at the top end. Our casino reviews note which providers each operator carries, and the most-played casino games in Canada gives a sense of how table games like this one sit alongside slots in Canadian lobbies.

How it compares to its relatives

If you enjoy the format, it is worth knowing that similar games in the same family often price better. Three Card Poker's ante-play combination and Casino Hold'em both offer lower edges against total money wagered, and video poker beats all of them if you are willing to learn a full strategy chart. Caribbean Stud earns its place through pace and the shape of its payouts rather than through value.

The bottom line

Caribbean Stud rewards a small amount of discipline with a meaningful improvement in results. Raise every pair, fold everything below ace-king, apply the upcard rules in between, and leave the progressive alone unless you have decided in advance that you are buying a lottery ticket. Do that consistently and you are playing a mid-tier table game at its best available price — which is all any casino game can honestly offer.

You must be 19+ (18+ in some provinces) to gamble in Canada. If gambling stops being fun, free confidential help is available in every province.
